docs.title: Service catalog
docs.text:
The ports below are the documented defaults. Web interfaces generally bind to loopback and are intended to be published through the configured reverse proxy. AdGuard Home uses host networking; WG-Easy additionally publishes its WireGuard UDP endpoint.

Service Default host endpoint Persistent host data Miniflux 127.0.0.1:8080 miniflux/db/ TimeTagger 127.0.0.1:8080 timetagger/ Grav 127.0.0.1:8080 grav/data/ Forgejo Web 127.0.0.1:8027, SSH 127.0.0.1:2222 forgejo/data/ Portainer 127.0.0.1:9000 portainer/data/ TasmoAdmin 127.0.0.1:8016 tasmoadmin/data/ Wallabag 127.0.0.1:8017 wallabag/data/, wallabag/images/ Vaultwarden 127.0.0.1:8018 vaultwarden/ NocoDB 127.0.0.1:8019 nocodb/data/ Homepage 127.0.0.1:8020 homepage/config/ Linkwarden 127.0.0.1:8021 linkwarden/postgres/, data/, meili/ WG-Easy UI :51821, WireGuard UDP :51820 wg-easy/ Paperless-ngx 127.0.0.1:8022 paperless/postgres/, data/, media/, consume/, export/ Firefly III App 127.0.0.1:8023, FinTS :8024 firefly-iii/ Snipe-IT 127.0.0.1:8025 snipe-it/database/, storage/ AppFlowy 127.0.0.1:8026 appflowy/postgres/, minio/, search/ MDMesh 127.0.0.1:8030 mdmesh/postgres/, server/, caddy/, backups/ AdGuard Home Host network; DNS TCP/UDP :53, setup :3000 adguard_home/conf/, work/

All paths in the table are relative to ~/.docker/. Services use host-directory bind mounts; Docker-managed named volumes are not used. Some supporting containers intentionally use ephemeral storage (for example, AppFlowy's Redis queue).

docs.title: How deployment works
docs.text:
01 · Configure

Add the service key below docker in host data. Secrets belong in the encrypted secrets file.

02 · Render

Compose is written to ~/.docker/<service>/docker-compose.yml; its user systemd unit is written under ~/.config/systemd/user/.

03 · Reconcile

Changed Compose configuration triggers an image pull and service reconciliation. Unchanged files do not cause an image pull.

04 · Operate

systemd manages start, restart and stop. Registered assets can trigger a restart only when they actually change.

  • Enable Docker services by setting docker to a truthy mapping. tasks/docker.py installs Docker and defines the shared deployment helper; tasks/docker_container.py dispatches configured service modules.
  • Compose projects run as the configured user. Without Sablier, deployment uses docker compose up -d; with Sablier, it prepares containers using docker compose up --no-start.
  • stop_dependencies controls whether stopping a systemd unit stops the complete Compose project or only its configured app_services.
  • Image updates are change-triggered. To update an image without changing configuration, run an intentional manual pull for that service.
  • Service modules can register extra restart triggers for generated assets. Homepage, for example, is restarted when synchronized public icons change.

docs.title: Storage and security
docs.text:
~/.docker/<service>/

Compose files, environment files and persistent application data stay grouped per service.

Host bind mounts only

Data is visible and backup-friendly on the host. No Docker-managed named volumes are used.

Encrypted secrets

Passwords, API keys and signing secrets belong in secrets.json.gpg, not tracked host data.

Loopback by default

Publish web interfaces through a trusted reverse proxy or VPN rather than exposing container ports publicly.

Before enabling a service

Check for existing listeners and reverse-proxy routes, configure strong secrets, and review the Compose template. Portainer, MDMesh's supervisor and other Docker-socket consumers can control the Docker host and must be treated as privileged components.

docs.title: Sablier
docs.text: Sablier can start or resume labelled application containers on demand. It is enabled separately with docker_sablier.enabled; the tracked example disables it. Dynamic mode serves a waiting page while a service starts. The default provider strategy is pause, which preserves memory usage while idle; stop releases memory but causes a cold start. Sablier and the Docker battery monitor are mutually exclusive.

docs.title: Docker Power
docs.text: The optional battery monitor can stop configured containers to reduce power use. When Sablier is enabled, the monitor is disabled and containers it previously stopped are restored. See Task reference for the task gates and implementation details.

docs.title: Service configuration and operational notes
docs.text:
The task reference explains Homepage widgets, Linkwarden bookmark synchronization, Caddy/Dehydrated integration, AdGuard setup, MDMesh bootstrap behavior, service secrets and per-service configuration.

Detailed service notes and integration configuration

Service-specific notes

  • MDMesh is an Android-only MDM (it does not manage Linux endpoints) and is optional: it is deployed only when docker.mdmesh.domain is configured; leave the key unset to skip it. It deploys the upstream PostgreSQL 14, server, web-edge and supervisor images at the resolved docker.mdmesh.version (defaults to "latest"; a semantic version can be pinned). The web edge binds only to 127.0.0.1:8030 by default; add the public hostname to caddy_config, for example "mdm.example.com:443": {"reverse_proxy": "127.0.0.1:8030"}, so the existing Caddy instance terminates HTTPS. Set docker.mdmesh.domain to the same hostname. All persistent data, including PostgreSQL, server state, Caddy state/configuration and supervisor backups, uses host bind mounts under ~/.docker/mdmesh/; there are no Docker-managed named volumes. Store database_password, hash_secret and admin_password under secrets.docker.mdmesh in the encrypted secrets file; each must be at least 32 characters and must not contain quotes, backslashes or line breaks. The initial administrator is admin_email (default admin@<domain>) and must change the configured initial password at first sign-in. The task downloads the database seed and repair scripts from the same tagged MDMesh release, seeds only a fresh database, refuses an inconsistent database, and checks enrollment defaults before skipping the bootstrap operation on later runs. The supervisor mounts the Docker socket and can control host containers; treat it as a privileged component. Set trusted_proxies only to the actual CIDRs used by the existing reverse proxy. MDMesh's signed release/update mechanism is retained, but automatic updates are disabled; with version: "latest", the task resolves the latest stable release on each deployment and reconciles the images and bootstrap assets together. Pin a semantic version when a fixed release is required. Sablier is forcibly disabled for MDMesh, even when the global integration or a per-service opt-in is enabled: Android devices need an always-available management endpoint, and Sablier's lazy-start preparation leaves its containers created but stopped.

  • AppFlowy deploys the current AppFlowy Self-Hosted Commercial Compose stack (Cloud, GoTrue, PostgreSQL/pgvector, Redis, MinIO, AI, Worker, Search, Web, Admin and Nginx). Nginx binds only to 127.0.0.1:8026 and Caddy publishes appflowy.21x9.org. PostgreSQL, MinIO and Search data use direct bind mounts under ~/.docker/appflowy/; no Docker-managed named volumes are used. The task renders a private ~/.docker/appflowy/.env (mode 0600) from encrypted secrets.docker.appflowy values. Set postgres_password, admin_password, jwt_secret, minio_access_key and minio_secret_key; URL-interpolated secrets must use the documented URL-safe formats. Change the initial administrator password after first login. Cloud uses APPFLOWY_REDIS_URI, AI uses AI_REDIS_URL, Worker uses APPFLOWY_WORKER_REDIS_URL, and Search receives both APPFLOWY_INDEXER_REDIS_URL and APPFLOWY_SEARCH_REDIS_URL, mapped to the same Compose redis service endpoint rather than container-local localhost. Redis follows the upstream ephemeral configuration and has no persistent data mount or AOF; pending queue state may not survive Redis replacement. AppFlowy Self-Hosted Commercial is distributed under AppFlowy's commercial self-hosted license; review its terms before deployment. Homepage receives only a normal link, not an API widget or authenticated exporter.

  • Paperless-ngx runs with PostgreSQL 17, Valkey, Gotenberg and Tika. PostgreSQL data and Paperless data, media, consume and export directories are host bind mounts under ~/.docker/paperless/; no Docker named volumes are used. The directories are created idempotently with PostgreSQL ownership 70:70 and Paperless ownership controlled by docker.paperless.uid / gid (defaults to 1000:1000). Its web interface binds to 127.0.0.1:8022 and the supplied local Caddy configuration publishes paperless.21x9.org. Store postgres_password (URL-safe) and secret_key under secrets.docker.paperless in the encrypted secrets file. Generate a strong secret key and do not leave the example placeholders in place. The host import directory ~/Paperless is a symlink to ~/.docker/paperless/consume; place documents there to import them.

  • Firefly III runs with MariaDB, an Alpine cron container and the FinTS importer. The application binds to 127.0.0.1:8023 (firefly.21x9.org) and the importer UI to 127.0.0.1:8024 (fints.21x9.org). Database files, Firefly uploads and importer configurations are host bind mounts under ~/.docker/firefly-iii/; no named volumes are used. Store database_password, mysql_root_password, app_key and the exactly 32-character cron_token under secrets.docker.firefly-iii in the encrypted secrets file. Use a Laravel-compatible application key (for example, a base64:-prefixed 32-byte key). The importer is the community benkl/firefly-iii-fints-importer image; after first start, open its UI, set the Firefly III URL to http://app:8080 from within the Compose network, and provide a Firefly III personal access token. The importer stores its bank connection configurations under ~/.docker/firefly-iii/fints/. FinTS authentication data is sensitive; protect access to the importer hostname and host directory accordingly.

  • Snipe-IT runs with MariaDB 11.4 and the official snipe/snipe-it image. Its database and application storage use direct host bind mounts from ~/.docker/snipe-it/database/ and ~/.docker/snipe-it/storage/, respectively. The backing directories are prepared idempotently with MariaDB ownership 999:999 and Snipe-IT ownership 10000:50. The application binds to 127.0.0.1:8025 and the supplied local Caddy hostname is snipeit.21x9.org. Store database_password, mysql_root_password and a generated Laravel app_key under secrets.docker.snipe-it in the encrypted secrets file. Generate the key with docker compose run --rm app php artisan key:generate --show; keep the same key for the lifetime of the installation.

  • Miniflux uses a PostgreSQL companion container. Its database is persisted in ~/.docker/miniflux/db/; administrator and database credentials are read from secrets.docker.miniflux.
  • TimeTagger stores its data in ~/.docker/timetagger/, mounted at the container's /root/_timetagger directory.
  • Grav persists the complete web application data directory in ~/.docker/grav/data/. Its setup, scheduler and fix_permissions options are configurable.
  • Forgejo persists application data in ~/.docker/forgejo/data/. Its web and SSH ports bind to loopback by default; the public domain is configurable. The HTTP host port defaults to 8027 while the container continues listening on 3000. Override it with docker.forgejo.port if needed, and point the corresponding Caddy reverse_proxy to the same loopback host port (for example 127.0.0.1:8027). Existing explicit port: 3000 host settings are not migrated automatically; update that setting and the Caddy route together to resolve a conflict.
  • Portainer persists data in ~/.docker/portainer/data/ and mounts /var/run/docker.sock. Access to Portainer effectively grants administrative control over the Docker host; expose it only through a trusted, authenticated reverse proxy.
  • TasmoAdmin mounts ~/.docker/tasmoadmin/data/ at /data/tasmoadmin, matching its TASMO_DATADIR setting.
  • Wallabag uses SQLite and persists its database/application data and article images in the two host directories shown above. The directories are mounted into the container paths used by Wallabag's www-data process. The supplied local Caddy configuration publishes it as wallabag.21x9.org; the initial credentials are wallabag / wallabag, which must be changed after first login.
  • Vaultwarden persists its data in ~/.docker/vaultwarden/. Public signups and invitations are disabled. An optional Argon2 PHC admin-token hash is read from secrets.docker.vaultwarden.admin_token; generate it with docker run --rm -it vaultwarden/server:latest /vaultwarden hash. Its supplied local Caddy hostname is vaultwarden.21x9.org.
  • NocoDB persists application data in ~/.docker/nocodb/data/, mounted at /usr/app/data. Its HTTP interface binds to loopback on port 8019 by default; the supplied local Caddy hostname is nocodb.21x9.org.
  • Linkwarden uses PostgreSQL 16 and Meilisearch alongside the application. Three host bind mounts store PostgreSQL data, Linkwarden archives/uploads and the Meilisearch index in ~/.docker/linkwarden/postgres/, ~/.docker/linkwarden/data/ and ~/.docker/linkwarden/meili/, respectively. Its web interface binds to loopback on port 8021; the supplied local Caddy hostname is linkwarden.21x9.org. Database, NextAuth and Meilisearch secrets are read from secrets.docker.linkwarden; use distinct, URL-safe values for all three secrets. NEXTAUTH_URL is generated as https://linkwarden.21x9.org/api/v1/auth (or the configured domain). All three directories are mounted directly from the host. The manual Homepage bookmark synchronizer supports docker.linkwarden.blacklist for bookmark IDs and docker.linkwarden.exclude_categories for collection names; category matching ignores case and surrounding whitespace. Both lists default to empty. Run python tasks/docker/linkwarden_bookmarks.py --dry-run to preview the result before synchronization. Run python tasks/docker/linkwarden_bookmarks.py --list-links to print every Linkwarden link ID, category, title and URL in a tab-separated table for copying IDs into the blacklist. Listing is read-only and does not download favicons or modify files.
  • WG-Easy stores WireGuard configuration in a host bind mount at ~/.docker/wg-easy/; it publishes UDP 51820 for VPN traffic and binds its administration UI to 127.0.0.1:51821. The UI is reverse-proxied through Caddy at vpn.21x9.org. Complete the initial setup wizard to set the public endpoint to vpn.21x9.org and create the administrator account. INSECURE=true is set only for the HTTP connection between the container and the local Caddy reverse proxy; do not publish the UI port directly.
  • Homepage stores its configuration in ~/.docker/homepage/config/, mounted at /app/config. It binds to loopback on port 8020 and sets HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS to the configured hostname; the supplied local Caddy hostname is homepage.21x9.org. Optional host-data keys settings, services, bookmarks, widgets, docker, kubernetes and proxmox are rendered to their matching *.yaml files. Each file is rendered only when its key is present; omitted sections are left untouched. The supplied group_data/@local.py includes service links to locally deployed applications and grouped bookmarks. Bookmark categories include Misc (GitHub, Kachelmannwetter, dict.leo, docsbot and lookscanned), Social (Reddit, Mastodon, Discord and LinkedIn), Entertainment (YouTube, Last.fm and Letterboxd), and Proton (Mail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, VPN, Pass, Authenticator, Wallet, Meet and Lumo). Icons are referenced as local files under /icons/; they are not fetched from third-party favicon URLs at dashboard runtime. The icons are stored in files/homepage/icons/ and synchronized idempotently to ~/.docker/homepage/public/icons/; synchronization does not delete destination files, so local-only icons are preserved. Homepage is restarted only when this synchronization changes files, ensuring newly deployed icons are picked up without causing unnecessary restarts on unchanged runs. The public asset directories use mode 0755; icon synchronization does not enforce per-file ownership or permissions, avoiding repeated metadata changes if the Homepage container adjusts mounted asset metadata. The Compose service mounts the icon and image directories separately at /app/public/icons and /app/public/images. Set each service's icon to a path such as /icons/miniflux.png. Configure the dashboard background under docker.homepage.settings.background; the local example uses the official Homepage sample image hosted by Unsplash. Replace the URL or use a local image such as /images/background.jpg stored in ~/.docker/homepage/public/images/. Homepage also supports blur, saturate and brightness background options. The local example configures settings.layout.Services with style: row and columns: 3, arranging service cards in three columns. Adjust the column count in host data to suit the display. Docker socket access is not enabled by default. Homepage dashboards may expose sensitive widget data, so protect access with a trusted reverse proxy authentication policy, Homepage authentication, or a VPN.

Homepage supports two distinct widget types: service widgets are configured inside each service entry in services.yaml, while header/info widgets are configured in widgets.yaml. Both are supplied through the docker.homepage.services and docker.homepage.widgets host-data keys. The local example enables: - FRITZ!Box status, uptime and transfer rates at 192.168.42.1. Enable Allow access for applications and Transmit status information over UPnP in the FRITZ!Box network settings. The widget does not require credentials and supports at most four fields. - Miniflux unread/read article counts. Create an API key under Miniflux Settings → API keys. - Forgejo repository, notification, issue and pull-request counts using Homepage's Gitea-compatible widget. Create an API token with notifications, repository and issue permissions. - Portainer running/stopped/total container counts. Create an API access token and verify the environment ID (1 in the supplied example) in Portainer. - OpenWeatherMap current weather and forecast for Cologne, Germany, configured with metric units and a five-minute cache. Homepage reads the API key from the shared settings.providers.openweathermap entry, which resolves HOMEPAGE_VAR_OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY from the container environment. Store the key under secrets.docker.homepage.environment in secrets.json.gpg; an OpenWeatherMap One Call API subscription/key is required. See the OpenWeatherMap widget documentation. - Glances host metrics (CPU, memory, CPU temperature, uptime and the / filesystem). The Homepage task manages a system-level glances-web.service running as the configured deployment user; this avoids depending on an interactive user session or user D-Bus. When the unit changes, it restarts the service and removes only a stale Glances web-server process matching the configured user, bind address and port before starting the managed instance; the separate Glances server mode (-s) is not affected. Glances listens on Docker's host-gateway address (default 172.17.0.1:61208) and is reached using the Compose host.docker.internal:host-gateway mapping. The Homepage network's own gateway (for example 172.27.0.1) is not the address used by host.docker.internal. UFW access is managed centrally through the ufw configuration in group_data/@local.py: docker-host-glances allows the Homepage Docker subnet (172.27.0.0/16) to reach the Glances listener at the Docker host-gateway address (172.17.0.1:61208). The Homepage task does not add firewall rules itself. The API port is not published by Compose or opened to arbitrary source networks. If the Docker subnet, host-gateway address, Glances bind address or port changes, update the corresponding custom UFW rule to match docker.homepage.glances.bind_address and docker.homepage.glances.port. - A date/time widget using the German locale and 24-hour time format, and DuckDuckGo search. CPU, memory and filesystem metrics are provided by Glances to avoid duplicate resource displays.

The Miniflux, Forgejo and Portainer service widgets use their public HTTPS hostnames (rss.21x9.org, forgejo.21x9.org and portainer.21x9.org) as API URLs. The Homepage Compose template maps these names to Docker's host-gateway address with extra_hosts; this prevents container DNS from resolving a public hostname to the host's loopback address (127.0.0.1). Caddy receives the HTTPS requests on the host gateway and routes them by hostname to the services bound to host loopback ports. Keep Caddy reachable on the host-gateway interface on port 443. The host.docker.internal mapping remains available separately for host services such as Glances. Homepage substitutes {{HOMEPAGE_VAR_*}} placeholders from its environment. The example secrets.json.gpg.example documents HOMEPAGE_VAR_MINIFLUX_API_KEY, HOMEPAGE_VAR_FORGEJO_API_KEY, HOMEPAGE_VAR_PORTAINER_API_KEY and HOMEPAGE_VAR_OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY under hosts.@local.docker.homepage.environment; tasks/docker/homepage.py merges this secret mapping into the container environment, with secret values taking precedence. Keep the actual API keys only in the encrypted secrets file, never in @local.py. The Portainer widget's env: 1 refers to the example environment ID; change it if the Portainer environment has a different ID.

Optional integrations: Homepage also supports widgets for WGEasy, Grafana, Home Assistant and Paperless-ngx. These applications are not deployed by this repository's Docker service tasks (Grafana, Home Assistant and Paperless-ngx are referenced only as external LAN services; WG-Easy is deployed by this repository, but its Homepage widget is not enabled in the supplied local configuration). Add them as service entries only when the corresponding application is reachable from the Homepage container. For WGEasy v15 and newer, use widget type wgeasy, version 2, and the configured username/password; older releases use API version 1. See the WGEasy widget documentation. The FRITZ!Box, Miniflux, Forgejo/Gitea and Portainer widget schemas are documented in the Homepage service widget reference.

Example optional service entries (add them to a group in docker.homepage.services and replace the URLs and credentials with values reachable from the Homepage container):

        "href": "https://wg-easy.example.org",
        "widget": {
            "type": "wgeasy",
            "url": "http://wg-easy:51821",
            "version": 2,  # WGEasy v15+

            "password": "{{HOMEPAGE_VAR_WGEASY_PASSWORD}}",        },

},

        "widget": {

            "version": 2,  # Grafana > 10.4
            "url": "http://grafana:3000",
            "username": "{{HOMEPAGE_VAR_GRAFANA_USERNAME}}",
            "password": "{{HOMEPAGE_VAR_GRAFANA_PASSWORD}}",
        },

},
{

        "href": "https://ha.example.org",
        "widget": {
            "type": "homeassistant",
            "url": "http://homeassistant:8123",
            "key": "{{HOMEPAGE_VAR_HOME_ASSISTANT_TOKEN}}",
        },
    },

        "widget": {

The local Homepage configuration declares the Miniflux, Forgejo and Portainer API-key environment variables with empty defaults. Store their actual values in secrets.docker.homepage.environment in secrets.json.gpg; tasks/docker/homepage.py merges that mapping over docker.homepage.environment, so secret values always take precedence. Do not put real credentials in tracked host-data files. For WGEasy v15 and newer, use widget type wgeasy and version 2; older releases use API version 1. See the WGEasy widget documentation, Grafana, Home Assistant and Paperless-ngx documentation.

Header widgets and service widgets can expose network and application data. Keep Homepage behind trusted authentication, a VPN, or an authenticated reverse proxy. API keys must have only the permissions needed for read-only dashboard access.

AdGuard Home

Enable it by adding an AdGuard Home mapping to docker in @local.py. It runs as a Docker Compose container using host networking, which lets DNS listen directly on host TCP/UDP port 53 without Docker port publishing. Persistent configuration and query data remain in the bind-mounted directories ~/.docker/adguard_home/conf/ and ~/.docker/adguard_home/work/. The default image is pinned to adguard/adguardhome:v0.107.80; override it with docker.adguard_home.image when deliberately upgrading.

Configure the web UI port with docker.adguard_home.web_port in @local.py. It defaults to 3000 when omitted; set it to 3001 if another service already occupies host port 3000. Forgejo now defaults to host port 8027:

docker = {
    "adguard_home": {
        "image": "adguard/adguardhome:v0.107.80",  # Pinned container image.
        "web_port": 3001,  # Host web UI port, different from another listener on 3000.
    },
}
caddy_config = {
    "adguard.example.com:443": {
        "reverse_proxy": "127.0.0.1:3001",
    },
}

On first start, complete AdGuard Home's setup wizard at http://<host-address>:3000 (the initial setup port remains AdGuard's default). After the configuration file exists, the task stops AdGuard before reconciling only http.address to 127.0.0.1:<docker.adguard_home.web_port>, preserving the rest of AdGuardHome.yaml; the normal deployment then restarts the service when the address changes. The first-run configuration is left untouched until the setup wizard creates the file. The web UI is then loopback-only and should be reached through the configured Caddy reverse proxy. The default port remains 3000 unless explicitly overridden.

DNS continues to use host TCP/UDP port 53. Configure DNS to listen only on the LAN and WireGuard addresses that should serve clients, then add DNS rewrites for the desired local names and aliases. Host networking means there are no Compose port mappings to restrict exposure. Check for an existing host resolver already using port 53 before enabling the container; do not disable or reconfigure the host resolver automatically. Point the FRITZ!Box DHCP DNS setting and/or WireGuard clients' DNS setting at the host's reachable AdGuard Home address. The container is opt-in and is not deployed unless docker.adguard_home is present.

Optional public DNS access: UFW custom rules can allow DNS from any source by adding "adguard-dns": {"action": "Allow", "rule": "53"} to the ufw mapping in @local.py. A port rule without a protocol suffix opens both TCP and UDP port 53, and UFW reports the source as Anywhere (including IPv6 when IPv6 support is enabled). This is intentionally not enabled by default. Exposing DNS publicly can create an open resolver and enable abuse or amplification attacks; configure AdGuard's allowed clients and recursion policy before enabling it. Do not expose the setup wizard or administration UI publicly.

Storage migration

All configured services use direct host bind mounts below ~/.docker/; no Docker-managed named volumes are used. When changing a service's storage definition, Docker Compose does not automatically migrate existing data. Back up the source and migrate its contents before switching templates. Existing data already in the documented host directories remains in place.

tasks/docker/ contains the service-specific configuration and templates/docker/ contains the corresponding Compose files. Consult both before changing a service's supported host-data keys or storage layout.

docs.title: Operational safety and idempotency
docs.text:
• Run a dry deployment and inspect the diff before applying changes.
  • Keep real host data and secrets out of Git. Tracked .example files are templates, not production configuration.
  • Review firewall, VPN, SSH, Samba, Docker socket and reverse-proxy changes for lockout or exposure risk.
  • Tasks should check current state before changing it. An identical second deployment should not report changes or restart services without a real reason.
  • Docker persistence uses explicit host bind mounts below the configured home directory's .docker/; Docker-managed named volumes are not used.
  • Installing backup tools is not a backup strategy: configure repositories, encryption credentials, schedules and restore tests separately.
  • A dry run is a planning aid, not rollback. Back up important state and retain console/out-of-band access for network changes.

docs.title: Pyinfra Manager (COSMIC desktop app)
docs.text: Pyinfra Manager is a native COSMIC desktop front end for this repository. It delegates deployment to the existing deploy.py entry point and does not duplicate pyinfra task logic.

docs.title: Using the application
docs.text:
1. Start Pyinfra Manager. It first checks PYINFRA_REPOSITORY, the last valid checkout saved under $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pyinfra-manager/repository (or ~/.config/pyinfra-manager/repository), the launch directory, and the executable's parent directories. You can also enter a checkout path directly in the path field. A valid checkout must contain deploy.py, inventory.py, pyproject.toml, group_data/, tasks/, and the manager backend. Valid paths are remembered for the next launch.
  2. Open Tasks and load the catalog. It includes literal includes from deploy.py, the workstation task loop parsed from that file, and Python modules found below tasks/. The entrypoint field distinguishes modules included by the deployment from implementation/helper modules.
  3. Open Settings to initialize and edit group_data/@local.py and group_data/workstation.py. The app opens the selected file with the desktop's configured editor.
  4. Use Validate both settings files after editing. Validation parses Python syntax only; it never imports or executes configuration.
  5. Select a host under Deploy and review Preview (dry-run) output. Applying changes is a separate two-step action.

The application currently runs the full deploy.py orchestration for the selected host. Feature inclusion remains controlled by the configuration gates in deploy.py; the task catalog is an inventory, not a second feature switchboard.

docs.title: Local backend
docs.text:
The Python backend is also usable independently:

uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py catalog
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py hosts
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py init-config
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py read-config local
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py validate-config local group_data/@local.py
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py run @local
uv run python apps/pyinfra-manager/backend/manager.py run @local --apply

The deployment command is a dry-run by default. The --apply flag is required to make changes.

docs.title: Settings and backups
docs.text:
The settings menu manages only these ignored local files:

  • group_data/@local.py — host-specific configuration.
  • group_data/workstation.py — shared workstation-role configuration.

Missing files are initialized from tracked .example templates without overwriting existing files. Before opening a file in an external editor, the backend creates a timestamped mode-0600 backup under $XDG_STATE_HOME/pyinfra-manager/backups (or ~/.local/state/pyinfra-manager/backups). Python syntax validation is available from the settings page. Configuration is never evaluated by the editor backend.

Credentials and private keys belong in the encrypted secrets workflow, not these settings files. The app does not add local configuration or backups to Git. Deployment output may contain sensitive host details and is kept local.

docs.title: Safety model
docs.text:
• Dry-run is the default; applying changes requires an explicit second action.
  • Only hosts declared in the literal _all_hosts inventory mapping are accepted by the backend.
  • Configuration file paths are allowlisted; symlinked config files and a symlinked group_data directory are rejected.
  • Settings syntax is parsed without evaluating arbitrary Python.
  • Backups are private and stored outside the repository.
  • Deployment output is not sent to telemetry or an external service.

docs.title: Building locally
docs.text:
Install Rust/Cargo and the native libraries listed by the libcosmic project, then build:

cd apps/pyinfra-manager
cargo build --release

The resulting executable is target/release/pyinfra-manager. Install resources/org.pyinfra.Manager.desktop into ~/.local/share/applications/ to add it to the desktop launcher. The app expects uv and the Python project dependencies to be available on the system, and it must be pointed at a pyinfra repository checkout.

docs.title: Local build checks
docs.text:
The repository has no GitHub Actions desktop-build workflow or downloadable Actions build artifact. Before building locally, check formatting and Clippy from the repository root:

cargo fmt --manifest-path apps/pyinfra-manager/Cargo.toml --all -- --check
cargo clippy --manifest-path apps/pyinfra-manager/Cargo.toml --all-targets -- -D warnings

Use the cargo build --release command above to create the Linux executable locally. Desktop entry and AppStream metadata are stored in apps/pyinfra-manager/resources/. The executable depends on installed COSMIC system libraries and the project's Python environment; it is not a self-contained installer.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: This repository is an infrastructure configuration project, not a distributable Python package. Releases are published as GitHub Releases; there is no PyPI publishing step.

docs.title: Create a release
docs.text:
1. Merge the changes intended for the release into main.
  2. Update CHANGELOG.md with a dated entry describing the changes.
  3. Ensure your local checkout is clean and up to date, then run the release helper from the repository root:
./scripts/publish-release.sh v1.2.3

The script verifies that: - the current branch is main; - the working tree is clean; - local main exactly matches the fetched origin/main; - CHANGELOG.md contains a dated release entry; and - the requested tag does not already exist locally or remotely.

It displays the release tag and commit and asks for confirmation before creating an annotated tag and pushing it to origin. If pushing fails, the local tag is retained so you can inspect the remote state before retrying.

  1. Create the GitHub Release manually from the pushed tag. Add release notes from the corresponding CHANGELOG.md entry.
  2. Review the published release at GitHub Releases.

Use vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tags. Pre-release and build metadata are accepted, for example v1.1.0-rc.1 and v1.1.0+build.2. The release process does not build or upload Python distribution artifacts. Merging a pull request does not publish a release; create the tag and GitHub Release explicitly when the changes are ready.

A tag is immutable release history: if a release needs correction, publish a new patch version rather than moving an existing tag.

docs.title: On-demand Samba file exchange
docs.text:
NETWORK FILE SHARING

Deploy and configure Samba shares with host-specific settings, controlled access and repeatable service management.

SharesDefine exported paths AccessManage users and permissions ServiceApply configuration safely

The optional Samba task provides two guest-accessible SMB shares for quick LAN/VPN file exchange:

  • Upload is a shared dropbox. Guests can upload and write files, but cannot delete or rename files. The directory uses the sticky bit and uploaded files inherit its root ownership. All guest connections use the same Unix identity (nobody), so this is not a private per-device inbox and users are not isolated from one another. Do not use it for confidential uploads.
  • Download is guest-readable and read-only. Publish files by copying them into the configured download directory on the server.

The task installs both the Samba server and smbclient, which provides a command-line client for testing guest share access directly from the server (for example, smbclient -N //127.0.0.1/Upload -c 'ls'). The service is deliberately not enabled at boot. On its first deployment, the task stops Samba and masks smbd.service; it does not start Samba or open the firewall. Starting Samba with samba-start creates a runtime marker so subsequent pyinfra deployments preserve that explicitly started session. samba-stop (including an idle-timeout stop) removes the marker, stops Samba and masks the service. The marker is stored under /run, so it is cleared on reboot. Run the deployed scripts when file exchange is needed:

sudo samba-start
# Connect from a client to \\server-address\Upload or \\server-address\Download
sudo samba-stop

On systems that provide /usr/share/samba/update-apparmor-samba-profile and the samba/smbd-shares AppArmor profile include, the task adds a systemd drop-in to run the helper before smbd starts. This regenerates the AppArmor permissions for the configured share paths without disabling AppArmor. Systems without this integration are left unchanged.

The scripts are safe to repeat. Start adds only missing UFW allow rules for the configured CIDRs, unmasks and starts smbd. Stop stops and masks smbd, then removes only matching rules found in UFW's added-rule list. TCP 445 is the only SMB port used; NetBIOS is disabled. The scripts manage UFW rules and therefore require UFW to be installed and active/configured on the host. If UFW is not the host firewall, adapt the scripts before use.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set a top-level samba mapping in host data:

samba = {
    "enabled": True,
    "interface": "enp3s0",
    "allowed_networks": ["192.168.1.0/24", "10.20.0.0/24"],
    "idle_timeout": 3600,  # 0 disables automatic shutdown
    "workgroup": "WORKGROUP",
    "server_string": "On-demand file exchange",
    "upload": {"path": "/srv/samba/upload"},
    "download": {"path": "/srv/samba/download"},
}
Key Default Description enabled False Opts into installation and configuration. interface lo Interface name Samba binds to, in addition to loopback. allowed_networks required Non-empty list of IPv4/IPv6 CIDRs allowed through UFW on TCP 445. idle_timeout 1800 Stop Samba after this many seconds without incoming SMB packets from allowed networks; any non-negative integer is accepted, and 0 disables automatic shutdown. Checks run every 60 seconds. workgroup WORKGROUP SMB workgroup. server_string On-demand file exchange Server description. upload.path /srv/samba/upload Persistent upload directory. download.path /srv/samba/download Persistent download directory.

Both paths must be distinct absolute paths. The task creates them if absent and never deletes their contents. Upload files and directories are owned by root with group nogroup; the upload directory and its subdirectories have the sticky bit set. This allows guests to create and write uploads while preventing the guest identity from deleting or renaming entries owned by root. Deployment conditionally migrates existing upload contents to these ownership and sticky-bit rules without changing file contents. Download files are not modified by Samba. Place files in the download directory using normal server-side tools and ensure they are world-readable.

When idle_timeout is greater than zero, samba-start installs a dedicated nftables counter and starts a systemd timer. The counter observes incoming TCP 445 packets on the configured interface from allowed CIDRs; unrelated interface traffic does not reset the timeout. The monitor checks every 60 seconds and stops Samba through samba-stop after the configured idle period. The default idle period is 30 minutes; any positive timeout is accepted. The monitor and its counter are removed when Samba is stopped manually or automatically. The idle monitor requires nftables (nft) and systemd.

The scripts are installed as /usr/local/sbin/samba-start and /usr/local/sbin/samba-stop. If /usr/local/sbin is not in the invoking user's PATH, call them by absolute path.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
This is intended only for a trusted LAN or VPN. Guest upload is intentionally frictionless, but all guests share one Unix identity and can write uploaded files. They cannot delete or rename entries protected by the sticky bit. Anyone with network access to TCP 445 can read the Download share and upload to Upload. Restrict allowed_networks to trusted CIDRs, do not forward TCP 445 from the internet, and stop the service when it is not needed. The firewall rules are temporary operational state: deployment does not open them, and samba-stop removes the matching rules.

The task does not create Samba user accounts, perform automatic cleanup, or automatically start the service after reboot.

docs.title: Secrets management
docs.text:
KEEP CREDENTIALS OUT OF GIT

Store passwords, API tokens and private keys in an encrypted secrets file, and manage it through the gpg-vault workflow.

GPGEncrypted at rest gpg-vaultCreate and edit safely RuntimeDecrypted only for deployment

The project stores sensitive values in a JSON document encrypted with GPG. Ordinary host configuration belongs in group_data/; credentials and private keys belong in the encrypted secrets document.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
File Purpose Commit? secrets.json.gpg.example Plaintext JSON example/schema with placeholder values Yes, after checking it contains no real secrets secrets.json Temporary plaintext working file No secrets.json.gpg Encrypted secrets consumed by deployment Normally no; keep outside version control

Both real secret files are listed in .gitignore.

The repository includes files/scripts/gpg-vault, an interactive helper deployed by tasks/scripts.py. It manages the plaintext/encrypted file pair locally; it does not change the JSON schema or the way pyinfra loads secrets. The repository also includes a Visual Studio Code extension for performing the same GPG operations from the editor.

docs.title: How loading works
docs.text:
common.initialize() checks for secrets.json.gpg using pyinfra's File fact. If found, it executes gpg --decrypt secrets.json.gpg, parses standard output as JSON, selects the current inventory host's secrets, and assigns the resolved dictionary to builtins.secrets. If the file is absent, builtins.secrets becomes {} and deployment continues.

Decryption failures and invalid JSON are not silently ignored: GPG errors and JSON parsing errors stop initialization. The GPG process may prompt for the passphrase depending on the local GPG agent configuration.

Docker service credentials are uploaded separately from Compose templates. The shared deploy_docker_service() helper writes private_env values to the service project's .env file with mode 0600. Values are written as single-quoted entries, so characters such as # are interpreted literally. Newlines, carriage returns, NUL bytes, single quotes and backslashes are rejected to keep the generated environment file unambiguous.

The environment file is not included in Compose template diffs, and a change to it triggers a service restart. AppFlowy generates its own .env file using the same restrictive file permissions.

docs.title: Supported top-level keys
docs.text:
The example file documents the current data shape:

Key Consumer Values shared.git_credentials tasks/git.py Git credentials inherited by every host unless overridden. hosts.<hostname>.wireguard tasks/wireguard.py Interface-indexed private keys and peer values, including optional preshared keys. hosts.<hostname>.dehydrated tasks/caddy.py Hetzner DNS API token used by Caddy's Dehydrated DNS-01 certificate workflow. hosts.<hostname>.docker.miniflux tasks/docker/miniflux.py Miniflux admin and PostgreSQL credentials. hosts.<hostname>.docker.paperless tasks/docker/paperless.py PostgreSQL password and Paperless secret key. hosts.<hostname>.docker.firefly-iii tasks/docker/firefly-iii.py MariaDB credentials, Laravel application key and 32-character cron token. hosts.<hostname>.docker.snipe-it tasks/docker/snipe-it.py MariaDB credentials and Laravel application key. hosts.<hostname>.docker.linkwarden Linkwarden deployment and Homepage bookmark sync PostgreSQL password, NextAuth secret and Meilisearch master key. hosts.<hostname>.docker.appflowy tasks/docker/appflowy.py PostgreSQL password, initial GoTrue administrator password, JWT secret, and MinIO access/secret keys. hosts.<hostname>.docker.homepage.environment tasks/docker/homepage.py, tasks/docker/linkwarden_bookmarks.py Homepage widget API keys/environment values, including the Linkwarden bearer API key reused by the bookmark synchronizer; encrypted values override host-data defaults. hosts.<hostname>.docker.timetagger tasks/docker/timetagger.py Required TimeTagger credentials value in username:bcrypt-hash format; written to ~/.docker/timetagger/.env with mode 0600 and excluded from Compose diffs. hosts.<hostname>.docker.vaultwarden tasks/docker/vaultwarden.py Optional Argon2 PHC hash for the Vaultwarden admin token (admin_token). hosts.<hostname>.ssh tasks/ssh_keys.py Default and per-key passphrases.

docs.title: Shared and host-specific values
docs.text:
The document has two top-level sections:

  • shared: values inherited by every inventory host.
  • hosts: values scoped to an exact pyinfra inventory hostname, such as @local or dns.

At initialization, common.py recursively merges the selected host's values over shared. Host-specific scalar values and lists replace shared values; nested objects are merged recursively. A host without an entry under hosts receives only the shared values. Secrets for other hosts are never included in the resolved dictionary.

Existing flat-format files remain supported for migration. Once migrated, keep all secrets under shared or hosts.<hostname>; do not mix legacy top-level secret categories with the new sections.

The inventory hostname must match the key under hosts exactly. This is the value exposed as host.name by pyinfra.

A secret entry alone does not necessarily activate a task. For example, WireGuard also needs wireguard_config in host data. See Deployment workflow.

docs.title: Example structure
docs.text:
Use secrets.json.gpg.example as the authoritative example. A simplified structure is shown below; replace every placeholder and remove categories you do not use.

{
  "shared": {
    "git_credentials": ["https://user:REPLACE_ME@git.example.net"]
  },
  "hosts": {
    "@local": {
      "dehydrated": {"hetzner_api_token": "REPLACE_ME"},
      "wireguard": {
        "wg0": {
          "privatekey": "REPLACE_ME",
          "peers": [{
            "PublicKey": "REPLACE_ME",
            "PresharedKey": "REPLACE_ME",
            "AllowedIPs": "0.0.0.0/0,::/0",
            "Endpoint": "vpn.example.net:51820",
            "PersistentKeepalive": 25
          }]
        }
      },
      "docker": {
        "vaultwarden": {"admin_token": "$argon2id$REPLACE_WITH_GENERATED_HASH"},
        "miniflux": {
          "admin_username": "admin@example.net",
          "admin_password": "REPLACE_ME",
          "postgres_password": "REPLACE_ME"
        }
      },
      "ssh": {
        "default_passphrase": "REPLACE_ME",
        "id_ed25519": {"passphrase": "REPLACE_ME"}
      }
    },
    "dns": {
      "dehydrated": {"hetzner_api_token": "REPLACE_WITH_DNS_TOKEN"}
    }
  }
}

Do not use the placeholder values in a real deployment. Avoid storing secrets in shell history or temporary files on shared systems.

docs.title: Manage secrets with gpg-vault
docs.text:
gpg-vault is installed as a user utility by tasks/scripts.py. Once files/scripts/ has been synchronized and the /usr/local/bin/ link created, run it from the repository root (or pass an explicit path with --file). It requires GPG and uses the executable named by $EDITOR, defaulting to nano.

gpg-vault create   # Create a new encrypted file in the editor
gpg-vault edit     # Decrypt, edit and re-encrypt
gpg-vault view     # Print decrypted contents to standard output
gpg-vault encrypt  # Encrypt secrets.json and remove plaintext on success
gpg-vault decrypt  # Decrypt to secrets.json
gpg-vault rekey    # Change the GPG passphrase
gpg-vault status  # Show file presence

The default pair is secrets.json and secrets.json.gpg. Select another plaintext filename by placing --file FILE before the command:

gpg-vault --file /path/to/credentials.json create
gpg-vault --file /path/to/credentials.json edit
gpg-vault --file /path/to/credentials.json status

create and edit stage plaintext in a private temporary directory and replace the encrypted file only after encryption succeeds. encrypt removes the source plaintext after successful encryption. decrypt refuses to overwrite an existing plaintext file and sets its mode to 0600. view writes decrypted data to the terminal; do not capture its output in logs. status reports file presence only, not passphrase or JSON validity.

The view and decrypt commands intentionally expose plaintext. Keep the terminal, filesystem and any resulting plaintext file secure. Temporary-directory cleanup is best-effort and does not replace sound host security or backups.

docs.title: Use the VS Code extension
docs.text:
The vscode/gpg-vault/ directory contains a standalone VS Code extension. It provides Command Palette commands to encrypt or decrypt the active local file, toggle a file between encrypted and decrypted states, and encrypt or decrypt selected text. The toggle command is also bound to Ctrl+Alt+E on Windows/Linux and Cmd+Alt+E on macOS. A .gpg file can also be decrypted from the VS Code Explorer context menu.

The extension invokes the local GPG executable and delegates passphrase entry to GPG Agent/pinentry; it does not store passphrases in VS Code. Both the VS Code extension and the command-line gpg-vault helper use symmetric AES-256 and produce ASCII-armored ciphertext (-----BEGIN PGP MESSAGE-----). Both use standard GPG decryption and remain compatible with existing binary GPG ciphertext.

File encryption saves the active document first, writes or replaces the sibling .gpg file without an overwrite prompt, and then removes the plaintext source. It attempts to overwrite the regular plaintext file with random data and flush it before unlinking, but this is best-effort sanitization rather than a guarantee of physical erasure. File decryption writes the original filename and replaces an existing plaintext destination without prompting. Decrypted files are created with owner-only permissions where supported. The gpg-vault.openDecryptedFile setting (default true) controls whether the decrypted file is opened in the editor; gpg-vault.gpgPath selects the GPG executable.

Selection commands replace the selected text in the editor with its encrypted or decrypted form. The extension stages operation data in a private temporary directory and removes that directory after the operation. See the extension README for installation and command details.

docs.title: Manual GPG fallback
docs.text:
The helper wraps symmetric AES-256 GPG encryption. If it is unavailable, the basic operations are:

gpg --symmetric --cipher-algo AES256 --output secrets.json.gpg secrets.json
gpg --decrypt secrets.json.gpg | python -m json.tool >/dev/null

For manual workflows, verify encrypted output before deleting plaintext. shred cannot guarantee secure erasure on every filesystem, SSD, snapshotting storage or backup system. Prefer encrypted storage and minimize plaintext lifetime. Ensure secrets.json.gpg has restrictive permissions (chmod 600 secrets.json.gpg). Keep a secure backup of the previous encrypted file until the new one has been verified and deployed.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• Never commit secrets.json or secrets.json.gpg.
  • Keep the example file free of real credentials.
  • Use a strong, unique GPG passphrase and protect access to it.
  • Restrict filesystem permissions on both encrypted and plaintext files.
  • Do not print secret values in task logs or error messages.
  • Rotate credentials immediately if they are exposed.
  • Review backups, editor swap files, temporary directories and shell history for accidental plaintext copies.
  • Do not assume that encryption makes a credential-bearing URL safe to share once decrypted.

docs.title: System configuration
docs.text:
MANAGE THE LINUX BASELINE

Configure operating-system settings such as hostname, locale, timezone, keyboard, kernel parameters and device security.

IdentityHostname, locale and users HardwareKeyboard, udev and USBGuard Kernelsysctl and system defaults

tasks/system.py manages operating-system settings from the current target's host.data. It is included in every full deployment. The supplied implementation targets Debian/Ubuntu-style system configuration files and Linux system facilities. The gpg-vault utility is deployed separately as a user script and does not change these system settings; see Secrets management.

docs.title: Settings overview
docs.text: Setting Type Default / behavior Purpose hostname string No change when absent System hostname. timezone string No change when absent System timezone identifier. locale string or None en_US.UTF-8 System-wide UTF-8 locale; None skips management. editor string No change when absent EDITOR environment setting. visual_editor string Falls back to editor VISUAL environment setting. keyboard dictionary {} XKB keyboard settings; empty disables management. sysctl dictionary {} Kernel parameters; empty disables management. udev dictionary {} Rule filename to rule-content mapping. usbguard dictionary Disabled unless enabled USB device authorization policy.

docs.title: Hostname and timezone
docs.text:
hostname = "node01"
timezone = "Etc/UTC"

The task validates the configured values and uses pyinfra server operations to apply them. Use a valid hostname and a timezone name from the system timezone database.

docs.title: Locale
docs.text:
locale = "en_US.UTF-8"
# Set to None to skip locale management.

The task checks /etc/default/locale, enables the requested locale when necessary, and maintains the LANG setting. The configured locale must use UTF-8 encoding. The custom SystemLocale fact inspects the current setting. Timezone comparison uses pyinfra's built-in server.Timezone fact and resolves /etc/localtime against the requested zoneinfo file. Aliases that resolve to the same file (for example, UTC and Etc/UTC) do not trigger repeated changes; server.timezone is scheduled only when the effective timezone differs.

docs.title: Default editors
docs.text:
editor = "vim"
visual_editor = "code --wait"

The task maintains EDITOR and VISUAL in /etc/environment. If visual_editor is not set, it uses the editor value.

docs.title: Keyboard layout
docs.text:
keyboard = {
    "layout": "us",
    "model": "pc105",
    "variant": "",
    "options": "",
}

Supported fields are layout, model, variant and options. Defaults are us, pc105, empty and empty respectively. The task writes /etc/default/keyboard. An empty dictionary disables management; when enabled, layout must not be empty.

docs.title: Kernel parameters (sysctl)
docs.text:
sysctl = {
    "net.ipv4.ip_forward": 1,
    "vm.swappiness": 10,
}

Each key is a kernel parameter and each value is its desired value. The task validates names and values, applies parameters immediately, and persists them in /etc/sysctl.d/99-local.conf.

Accepted values are strings, integers, or non-empty lists of strings/integers. Booleans are rejected even though Python treats them as integers. Empty values and embedded newline/carriage-return characters are rejected. Parameter names must match [a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+.

docs.title: udev rules
docs.text:
udev = {
    "70-network-name.rules": '''
SUBSYSTEM=="net", ACTION=="add", ATTR{address}=="02:00:00:00:00:01", NAME="lan0"
'''
}

Each key is a rule filename and each value is the complete rule content. Filenames must begin with a two-digit priority and end in .rules, matching [0-9]{2}-[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+\.rules. The task writes rules under /etc/udev/rules.d/, sets root ownership and mode 0644, and reloads udev rules when a file changes. An empty dictionary disables rule management.

docs.title: USBGuard
docs.text:
USBGuard applies a policy to USB devices. A restrictive policy can block essential input devices or remote administration hardware; prepare and validate rules before enabling it.

usbguard = {
    "enabled": True,
    "implicit_policy": "block",
    "present_device_policy": "apply-policy",
    "rules": [
        "allow id 1d6b:0002",
        "allow id 1d6b:0003",
        "allow id 1050:0407",
    ],
}

The example IDs are illustrative only. Generate and review rules for the actual hardware.

Parameter Type Default Accepted values / meaning enabled boolean False Install and enable the USBGuard daemon. implicit_policy string block allow, block or reject for devices without a matching rule. present_device_policy string apply-policy allow, block, reject, keep or apply-policy. rules list of strings [] Explicit authorization rules. Required and non-empty when enabled.

Rules must begin with allow, block or reject and must not contain embedded newlines or null characters.

The task manages:

Path Purpose Mode /etc/usbguard/ Configuration directory 0700 /etc/usbguard/usbguard-daemon.conf Daemon configuration 0600 /etc/usbguard/rules.conf Device policy 0600

The daemon configuration uses /etc/usbguard/rules.conf, the configured implicit/present-device policies, PresentControllerPolicy=keep, InsertedDevicePolicy=apply-policy and IPCAllowedUsers=root. USBGuard is installed through APT. Configuration changes cause the service to be enabled and restarted; otherwise the task ensures it is enabled and running.

docs.title: Add a USB device safely
docs.text:
1. Ensure you have a recovery path and that essential keyboard/mouse/controller devices have rules.
  2. Inspect devices with sudo usbguard list-devices.
  3. Temporarily authorize the intended device with sudo usbguard allow-device <ID>.
  4. Inspect the active policy using sudo usbguard list-rules.
  5. Add the reviewed rule to usbguard["rules"] in the relevant group-data file.
  6. Run a dry deployment, then apply and verify.

A runtime permanent authorization does not update the pyinfra source configuration. The next deployment may restore the rules from group data.

Useful commands:

Command Purpose sudo usbguard list-devices List connected devices. sudo usbguard list-devices -b List blocked devices. sudo usbguard list-devices -a List allowed devices. sudo usbguard list-rules Show active rules. sudo usbguard generate-policy Generate an initial policy from currently connected devices. sudo usbguard allow-device <ID> Temporarily allow a device. sudo usbguard allow-device -p <ID> Persistently allow a device in the runtime policy.

docs.title: Managed system files
docs.text:
Path Managed setting /etc/default/locale System locale (LANG). /etc/environment EDITOR and VISUAL. /etc/default/keyboard Keyboard layout. /etc/sysctl.d/99-local.conf Persistent kernel parameters. /etc/udev/rules.d/*.rules Custom udev rules. /etc/usbguard/usbguard-daemon.conf USBGuard daemon configuration. /etc/usbguard/rules.conf USBGuard authorization policy.

Hostname and timezone are managed through pyinfra operations rather than direct file writes.

docs.title: Validation and execution
docs.text:
The task validates hostnames, timezone identifiers, UTF-8 locale syntax, editor values, keyboard fields, sysctl keys/values, udev filenames/content, and USBGuard options/rules. Invalid configuration raises ValueError during task preparation.

Run only this task for focused testing:

pyinfra inventory.py tasks/system.py --dry --diff

For normal provisioning, use deploy.py so shared initialization and task selection are consistent. Always review changes to sysctl, udev and USBGuard carefully before applying them remotely.

docs.title: Task overview
docs.text: The deployment is composed of reusable Python modules under tasks/. The deploy entry point selects baseline tasks and optional features using inventory, host data and group data.

docs.title: Task areas
docs.text:
Area Examples Further information System foundations APT, users, sudo, hostname, locale, sysctl, udev, SSH keys, Git and fonts Core task reference Docker applications Compose services, directories, bind-mounted data, systemd units and integrations Docker guide Network and services WireGuard, VPN, Syncthing, Samba, UFW, Caddy, Dehydrated and AppArmor Optional task reference Workstation COSMIC settings, Flatpak, backups, power, firmware, storage, peripherals and developer tools Workstation features

The complete feature reference indexes the Python modules under tasks/, describes their inclusion conditions and documents relevant configuration.

docs.title: Docker conventions
docs.text:
Docker tasks are enabled through the docker host-data mapping. The shared Docker tasks configure the runtime and dispatch the service modules selected for the target.

  • Compose files and persistent application data are stored under ~/.docker/<service>/.
  • Persistent storage uses host bind mounts; Docker-managed named volumes are not used.
  • Web interfaces bind to loopback by default where applicable.
  • systemd user units manage Compose project lifecycle.
  • Sablier on-demand startup and the battery monitor are mutually exclusive options.

See the Docker guide for the service catalog, ports, data paths, secrets and operational behavior.

docs.title: Selecting and running tasks
docs.text:
Optional task inclusion is controlled by deploy.py and host or group data. Start with the configuration guide, check the feature reference and preview the deployment before applying it:

pyinfra inventory.py deploy.py --dry --diff

The preview should be reviewed for the intended hosts and operations. Apply only after checking the proposed changes and confirming that backups and access recovery are available where needed.

docs.title: Task reference
docs.text:
Run a consistent infrastructure workflow from one inventory: pyinfra's task modules turn host and group data into repeatable system configuration. Core tasks establish the baseline, optional tasks add services only when enabled, and workstation roles keep desktop-specific tooling separate.

Corebaseline on every full deployment Opt-inoptional features behind data gates Per hosthost and group configuration Repeatablechange-aware deployment operations

docs.title: Task groups
docs.text:
Core baseline

Packages, system settings, users' SSH and Git configuration, scripts, fonts and other essentials included in every full deployment.

Optional features

WireGuard, VPN activation, firewall rules, Docker services, Syncthing, Proton apps, browser extensions and other capabilities enabled through host data.

Workstation role

Explicitly enabled desktop and hardware features such as power management, firmware tools, storage utilities, peripherals and COSMIC settings.

Focused task runs

Run an individual task module for diagnosis or targeted work, while keeping the full deployment entry point for normal provisioning.

docs.title: How tasks are applied
docs.text:
01 · Inventory

Inventory membership and host/group data define the target machines and their desired configuration.

02 · Gate

deploy.py always includes core modules and evaluates feature flags before loading optional modules.

03 · Configure

Task modules use pyinfra operations and templates to install packages and manage system or user configuration.

04 · Reconcile

Change-aware operations avoid unnecessary restarts and updates; rerunning deployment converges toward the same state.

docs.title: Configuration model
docs.text:
Feature selection belongs in host or group data, not in edits to the task modules. Optional task gates are evaluated by deploy.py; workstation features additionally require their nested enabled: True setting.

# Example host/group data
wireguard_config = {...}  # enables WireGuard configuration
syncthing = True          # enables Syncthing
workstation = {
    "power": {
        "enabled": True,
        "manager": "tlp",
    },
}

Keep credentials and other sensitive values in the encrypted secrets file. Review each feature's configuration and operational notes before enabling it, especially for network access, firewall policy, VPN routing and privileged containers.

docs.title: Task reference
docs.text: The sections below describe the task modules, their inclusion conditions and the configuration keys they consume. Treat the implementation and templates as authoritative when checking accepted values or exact behavior.

docs.title: Core tasks
docs.text:
These task modules are included on every full deployment.

Module Responsibility Main configuration tasks/apt.py Downloads configured repository keys, writes APT source lists, updates package indexes, upgrades packages when the index changes, and installs packages. apt_sources, apt_packages tasks/hosts.py Manages /etc/hosts mappings. hostnames tasks/sudo.py Writes custom sudoers rules to /etc/sudoers.d/99-local, validates with visudo, and sets restrictive permissions. sudoers_rules tasks/system.py Manages hostname, timezone, locale, editor environment, keyboard, sysctl, udev and USBGuard. See System configuration. tasks/ssh_keys.py Generates supported SSH keypairs only when both files are absent and manages authorized keys. Existing private keys are never overwritten; an incomplete keypair (only the private or public file exists) fails safely and requires manual repair. ssh_keys, ssh_authorized_keys, secrets.ssh tasks/git.py Installs/configures Git and deploys Git-related configuration and credentials when available. Git host data and secrets.git_credentials tasks/fonts.py Installs font packages; optionally downloads Powerline-patched fonts. powerline_fonts tasks/scripts.py Synchronizes files/scripts/ into the configured user's scripts directory and creates command links. This includes gpg-vault, the helper for managing secrets.json.gpg. Existing destination files not in the source are preserved. username, usergroup tasks/mc.py Installs and configures Midnight Commander. username, usergroup

docs.text:
Module Inclusion condition Responsibility tasks/flatpak.py Flatpak executable detected during initialization Installs configured Flatpak application IDs exclusively in the user's Flatpak installation, explicitly preferring the user-scoped Flathub remote when an app is available from multiple remotes; uses a sole alternative user remote when necessary, skips already-installed user apps, and updates/cleans up only user-scoped applications and runtimes. Device and folder sharing is configured separately in Syncthing. tasks/zsh.py zsh Installs/configures Zsh and playerctl, deploys a LiMusic-specific MPRIS helper, and displays the current track in HyFetch only while LiMusic is playing. Rejects unknown rule names, invalid actions and malformed custom-rule definitions instead of silently skipping firewall configuration. tasks/docker.py and tasks/docker_container.py docker Installs Docker, defines the shared Compose/systemd deployment helper, and dispatches configured container services, including AppFlowy. tasks/docker_power.py docker Deploys the Docker battery monitor and its systemd unit; validates configured docker_power_save container names before writing its shell configuration; disables the monitor and restores previously stopped containers when Sablier is enabled. tasks/docker_sablier.py docker and docker_sablier.enabled Deploys Sablier as a Docker container using the Docker provider and enables on-demand startup through Compose labels.
